summary: This standards-track document defines the cid: and mid: URL schemes, which refer to parts of a mail message or to messages by identifier. For example, an HTML part can point to another part of the same message. It was replaced by RFC 2392.

plainLanguage.summary: A page inside a package says see the picture in the same box, by using the label on that picture.

questions: how to reference attachment in html email
how do html emails embed images
subtitle: How to reference parts of email messages using cid: and mid: web addresses.

tldr.problem: Email messages can contain multiple parts (a message with images, for example), but HTML inside an email needs a way to refer to other parts in the same message or to other messages.
tldr.mechanism: The cid: (Content-ID) URL scheme refers to a specific body part within a message, while the mid: (Message-ID) scheme refers to entire messages or specific parts within named messages, allowing HTML to embed references to images or other message components.
tldr.outcome: These URL schemes enable rich multipart email, where HTML can reference attached images or other parts by their identifiers. RFC 2392 replaced this document.

today: RFC 2111 is Proposed Standard and was obsoleted by RFC 2392. The cid: and mid: URL schemes remain in use for email applications that support multipart messages with internal cross-references.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The cid: (Content-ID) and mid: (Message-ID) URL schemes allow references to messages and body parts of messages. The primary use is within a single multipart message, where one HTML body part might include embedded references to other parts of the same message.

For example, an HTML part can refer to an image contained elsewhere in the same message using a cid: URL, avoiding the need to attach the image separately or reference it by an external URL.
sections.plainLanguage: Email messages can have several parts, like a letter with pictures. These URL types let one part point to another part in the same message.

sections.title: The cid: and mid: URL Schemes
sections.content:
The cid: URL scheme takes the form cid:<content-id>, where the content-id is URL-encoded. It refers to a specific body part (MIME entity) by its Content-ID header value. The use of cid: URLs is generally limited to references to other body parts in the same message as the referring body part.

The mid: URL scheme takes the form mid:<message-id> or mid:<message-id>/<content-id>. With only a message-id, it refers to an entire message. With the appended content-id, it refers to a specific body part within that message. This long form was designed to support interoperability with message storage systems that do not index body parts independently of their context.

Both message-id and content-id must be globally unique. Characters not allowed in URLs (such as "/" in a message-id) must be hex-encoded using the %hh escape mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: A cid: address says "the picture inside this message with this label." A mid: address says "the message with this ID" or "the part with this label inside that message."

sections.title: Practical Examples
sections.content:
A common example is an HTML email that includes images. The HTML might contain <IMG SRC="cid:image-part@example.com"> to reference an image body part with Content-ID image-part@example.com. The email client retrieves the image from the message itself rather than from the network.

Another example is a message that points to a previous message using a mid: URL that includes both the message-id and a content-id, allowing a thread to build references across multiple emails. This is useful when a reply needs to refer to a specific part within an earlier message.
sections.plainLanguage: An email with a picture can say "show the picture labeled image-part@example.com from inside this message." A reply can point to a specific part from an earlier message.
